What if a fat tries to grab you while drowning or something in a boating accident?

Interesting. Luckily, in a boating accident there are a few things that are different from this scenario:

  • Water everywhere, total freedom of movement. So the fatty isn't blocking anything, not standing (floating) between life and death for others. People can just swim away.

  • If someone is really drowning, they're not reacting as you expect: They're normally head down, not flailing. If it's a loved one, you dive, grab, drag up, and if they start to flail you push away while they cough (no longer drowning); tell them to calm down, wait about 5-10 seconds, then re-engage. If they flail again, you kick away again.

Flailing is a sign of panic, not the actual drowning (but they might not be able to catch breath). In short, it's like saying "I'm choking!"; if you can Say Something, your air is clear so you're not choking. But you're in panic, can't breathe, etc. Like that, basically. Real drowning looks like this: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instinctive_drowning_response

However, let's say the totally unexpected happens: You are sailing. For some reason, there is a fat with you (in law?). The fat is not wearing proper life jacket. Boat crashes, people are in the sink. Presumably someone's radioed for help. You're treading. Suddenly, from nowhere, the fat strikes: Grabs you for dear life. What you do there is the basic lifeguard technique: Get away. Push, smack, punch, kick, but basically kick away from their body like you were about to launch yourself from the pool wall to start a swimming set: Feet plant, knees cocked; Launch away. Swim 3-4 meters away. If the launch doesn't work, again slap punch or kick them in the face, body in a desparate attempt to get away. This is what lifeguards do with anyone who flails/panics and tries to take them down. Even gymbros will panic and instinctual try to use the lifeguard as a stool to stand on. So the lifeguard kicks away, even if they have to lightly injure the person in the process.

That's one element. The other is this: If possible, take a deep breath before they get around you. Then swim downwards with all your might. Swim downwards, and a panicing person will instinctually let go. Use these two techniques together. Usually the latter is the one officially taught, but to get into a good state you may have to kick/slap away as well, especially if they grabbed you unexpectedly and you weren't engaging them. Lifeguards approaching a human to save them will take a deep breath first in case this happens, so they can swim downwards without kicking/punching. But in this scenario we'll say that Shamoo snuck up on you when you were assessing the situation, confirming positions of other humans/loved ones.

The difference is, after that, the lifeguard waits 5-10 seconds, yells at them to calm down, then re-engages. With a fat, you simply warn the others to stay back. Swim away. If any are left, toss them a preserver and a Kit Kat to soothe their hanger.

Mostly, don't get close enough to them where it can become an issue.

A slight case of overthinking the problem when simple science can deliver the optimum solution.

Facts.
The object in question is a large mass moving forward suspended about one meter above ground by two supports.
The supports in question are never fully in contact with the ground at the same time and are moving in a synchronous loop.
The control system on these objects can't normally correct fast enough for large errors.

Solution...
One must address some basic Newtonian concepts here. I will avoid using maths and calculus as I feel that the core principles transcend the requirements of basic education.
Simply put. Interrupting the objects locomotive apparatus in the correct manor will have the desired results.
There are two major points to which disruption can be applied during the objects locomotive loop.
The first and most effective is this.
As the leading foot is about to be placed on the ground you must displace it before it has the chance to splash down. This is best done by matching velocity with your own foot and quickly applying sideward displacement to their foot so that the direction is to the center of mass. So right foot would be displaced to the left. This will result in a catastrophic system failure where the objects mass will become overcome by inertia and gravity.
The second method involves interruption of the loop at the weight bearing structure is about to transfer it's load to the other one. At this point, by applying a load to the base of the structure by stepping on its foot you can again cause a cascading failure to overwhelm the object system resulting in a desire for the object to rapidly seek equilibrium at the point of ground.
I would recommend the first course of action as it can be followed up by successive applications in a short space of time.
